_what: Possible patterns: the same kind of thing as the patterns beside them, but ones nobody has proved yet. Each says what is probably happening now, why that is likely, which proved cases sit nearest to it, and what would turn it into cases or knock it down. None of them is evidence, none names a person or a company in the claim, and none is counted in any figure on this map.

items.title: The companies building frontier AI, inside the offices that would govern them
items.claim: The handful of companies building the largest AI systems are probably inside the bodies that would govern them - the safety institutes, the export-control desks, the procurement offices and the advisory boards - because almost everyone qualified to staff those bodies comes from the companies being governed.
items.rule: The map proves the whole mechanism in other industries, in both directions: policy shops that write a government's programme and then staff it, and an industry adviser appointed to chair the regulator whose cases against that industry were then dropped. AI has the conditions those cases needed and one more - a technical monopoly, where the people who can judge a system are the people who built it.
items.conditions: The bodies are new, small and staffed by secondment. The rules they write are voluntary, drafted in consultation with the firms, and the state is simultaneously the industry's largest customer. Export controls on chips are decided with the same firms advising on what the controls should cover.
items.documented: The map holds Heritage's Mandate for Leadership, with most of its proposals acted on, and Project 2025's authors staffing the administration they wrote for; PNAC's signatories taking ten posts in the government that went to war on their argument; a crypto adviser who became chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission, after which crypto lawsuits were dropped; and a fracking chief who became United States energy secretary.
items.would_show: An ethics or inspector-general finding on a secondment or a recusal, a procurement decision reversed over an undeclared interest, or the drafting record of a standard showing who wrote it.
items.would_refute: Secondments, recusals and drafting records being published, with the standards traceable to people outside the firms.

items.title: Gulf states holding the officials of the countries that arm them, after they leave office
items.claim: The Gulf states are probably holding more serving and former office-holders across Europe, North America and the Horn of Africa than has been charged, because buying someone's last job is cheaper than buying their current one and is not usually a crime.
items.rule: This is the most heavily proved shape on the map in its older form - a foreign state on the payroll of another state's rulers - and the money available for it has multiplied. The cases that have surfaced came out almost entirely by accident: a Belgian police raid, a Twitter internal audit, a leak. Nothing suggests the accidents found the whole of it.
items.conditions: Sovereign wealth funds and state airlines hire former ministers, intelligence chiefs and regulators openly, and the register of interests that would catch it often does not cover them. Arms purchases, port concessions and gas contracts run through the same relationships.
items.documented: The map holds Qatargate, where Qatar and Morocco are alleged to have paid members of the European Parliament through an NGO, and the vice-president charged in it; a Qatar and Amazon lobbyist who became United States attorney general; Saudi Arabia paying Twitter staff to look up critics; a United Arab Emirates spy chief's firm buying 49 percent of the Trump family crypto company; a former Al Jazeera journalist running Somalia's intelligence service; and Saudi Arabia's Special Committee keeping 2,700 Yemeni leaders on its payroll.
items.would_show: A lobbying-registration prosecution, a parliamentary standards finding, or a sovereign fund's own disclosure of who it has hired.
items.would_refute: Post-office employment registers covering state-owned employers, published and enforced.

items.title: The spyware industry inside the interior ministries and spy services that buy it
items.claim: The companies selling phone-interception tools are probably not merely selling to states but sitting inside them - staffed by the services' own retired officers, running the systems they sold, and in some countries holding the access they were supposed to supply.
items.rule: The map proves the strongest possible version of this once, and with intelligence services as the party doing it: two of them secretly owned the Swiss company that sold cipher machines to a hundred governments, and read what those governments wrote. A vendor placed inside a ministry is the same arrangement with the ownership reversed, and the industry recruits almost entirely from the services it sells to.
items.conditions: Procurement is classified, so neither the contract nor the operator is published. Maintenance means vendor staff with live access. The same ministry that buys the tool authorises its use and investigates its misuse.
items.documented: The map holds the CIA and the BND secretly owning Crypto AG; a Huawei Poland executive charged with spying alongside a former Polish security official; Saudi Arabia paying a Twitter manager for users' data; and an apartheid police spy who became deputy director of a Geneva aid fund.
items.would_show: A court or oversight body naming vendor employees with access, a leaked contract with the operating terms in it, or a prosecution after an unlawful interception.
items.would_refute: Interception contracts, operator identities and audit logs reaching a body outside the buying ministry.

items.title: China's united front work inside local councils and candidate selection, not only national politics
items.claim: China's united front organisations are probably reaching further down than the national scandals suggest - into city councils, party branches, candidate selection and diaspora associations in a dozen democracies - because that is the level where a few hundred votes decide an outcome and nobody is watching.
items.rule: The map already proves the method at the top and at the very bottom of the same system, which is the part usually missed: a navy admiral agreeing to work with the United Front, and a city council campaign in California run on Beijing's instructions. Local offices are cheap, carry planning and procurement powers, and are the usual route to national candidacy.
items.conditions: Local campaigns have little money and almost no vetting. Diaspora associations provide the volunteers and the donations. Foreign-interference registers, where they exist, are written for lobbyists and national parties.
items.documented: The map holds Mike Sun running an Arcadia council campaign on Beijing's orders; Taiwanese vice admiral Ko Cheng-sheng agreeing to work with China's United Front; Chinese military intelligence recruiting aides inside Taiwan's government; a Chinese citizen elected mayor of the Philippine town where an offshore gaming hub operated; and a Huawei lobbyist's associates alleged to have paid members of the European Parliament to sign a 5G letter.
items.would_show: A foreign-interference prosecution or a security service report naming a local party branch, a council, or a candidate selection.
items.would_refute: Donation and volunteer records at local level being checked and published, with inquiries finding the associations acting on their own.

items.title: The sanctioned oil fleet inside the registries, insurers and inspectors that make it legal
items.claim: The fleet moving sanctioned oil is probably inside the paperwork industry that licenses it - the flag registries, the insurers and the classification societies - because a tanker is stopped by a missing certificate, not by a navy.
items.rule: This is the one possible pattern here with no case on the map at all, which is why it is worth stating. The structure is unusually exposed: a state's power to register ships is often delegated to a private company operating from another country and paid per vessel, and the map proves repeatedly that a sovereign function sold to outsiders gets used by them.
items.conditions: A registration confers a nationality in a single decision. The customer wants speed and discretion, the operator is paid by volume, and the flag state may learn what it has flagged when a vessel is detained. Insurance certificates are accepted on their face at most ports.
items.documented: Nothing directly. What the map does prove is the adjacent thing, many times: a Belgian firm sent to trial over its cut of each Congolese passport, a businessman running Comoros's passport sales with a former president jailed over it, crime bosses obtaining Macedonian passports from interior ministry staff, and creditors' agents running a country's customs.
items.would_show: A flag state's own audit or a criminal case against registry staff, an International Maritime Organization finding on a registry acting without authority, or a detention report tracing a false certificate to the office that issued it.
items.would_refute: Registries publishing what they refuse and why, with beneficial ownership checked before a flag is granted.

items.title: The scam compounds inside the immigration desks, police and zone authorities that should close them
items.claim: The operators of industrial fraud compounds are probably holding the immigration officers, police commanders and special-zone authorities of several South East Asian states, because a compound cannot run without people crossing borders and nobody raiding the gate.
items.rule: This is the shape the map already proves in three of the countries concerned, and a compound needs more official cover than a drug shipment does: staff trafficked in, victims held in, money moved out, and a perimeter nobody enters. The industry is now estimated in the tens of billions a year, which is more than the budgets of the agencies supposed to stop it.
items.conditions: Many compounds sit in special economic zones or border enclaves with their own authorities, their own security and their own entry rules, where the body that licenses the zone is also the body that would have to raid it.
items.documented: The map holds a Chinese citizen elected mayor of the Philippine town where an offshore gaming hub operated; the builders of a Myanmar scam city working with the army's Karen border force; an online gambling network reported to be protected by a Thai deputy police chief; 80 Thai immigration officers charged over Chinese crime groups; and a Vietnamese gambling ring with two senior police chiefs as backers.
items.would_show: A prosecution naming a zone authority or an immigration post, an Interpol or United Nations operation with officials arrested, or a defector's account that names the arrangement rather than the camp.
items.would_refute: Raids reaching the operators while the officials around them turn out to have been bypassed rather than bought.

items.title: The security companies taking the adviser's chair, now that one of them has shown it works
items.claim: Armed security companies beyond Wagner are probably taking posts beside presidents and inside defence ministries in exchange for mineral and customs concessions, because the arrangement has been demonstrated, paid for, inherited by a state, and never reversed.
items.rule: The map proves the full mechanism in one country, in detail: a company's man appointed the president's security adviser, the company's officers taking command of army units, its proxies given ministerial posts, and its firms granted mining permits with a report that they shaped the mining code. A model that worked and survived the death of the man who built it is the kind that gets copied, and the governments short of soldiers are not short of minerals.
items.conditions: A government fighting an insurgency can pay in concessions rather than cash, and the contract that supplies the soldiers can also supply the official who writes the next contract. Several of these companies are now owned or directed by the states they come from.
items.documented: The map holds Wagner's Valery Zakharov appointed security adviser to the Central African Republic's president, Wagner officers commanding Central African army units, Wagner proxies given ministerial posts there, Wagner firms granted mining permits with a report that they shaped the mining law, and Prigozhin's strategists paying Madagascar presidential candidates.
items.would_show: An appointment decree, a contract, or a United Nations panel finding naming a company's employee in a government post, with a concession to the same company.
items.would_refute: The successor companies turning out to be paid in cash on published contracts, with nobody placed in government.

items.title: The arms makers inside the offices now spending Europe's rearmament money
items.claim: The defence manufacturers are probably inside the bodies deciding how Europe's rearmament money is spent - the procurement agencies, the capability committees, the urgency exemptions - because the sums have multiplied while the offices deciding them have not.
items.rule: The map proves that these companies pay for decisions when the decisions are worth enough: commissions to a Saudi prince over Al-Yamamah, 115 million pounds of commissions over South Africa's arms deal, intermediaries used across Airbus's markets. It also proves the quieter version, which is the one to expect here: a government's own aircraft buyer taking a job with the company whose contracts she was handling.
items.conditions: Emergency procurement suspends competition and shortens publication. The specifications are written with industry in the room because only industry knows what is available. The officials who write them are recruited by the firms that bid.
items.documented: The map holds BAE paying a Saudi prince over the Al-Yamamah deals; BAE's 115 million pounds in commissions over South Africa's arms deal; Thales accused of paying Zuma through his adviser; Airbus paying intermediaries to bribe officials for contracts; and United States Air Force buyer Darleen Druyun taking a Boeing job while handling Boeing's deals.
items.would_show: An audit office or anti-fraud office report on an urgency exemption, a revolving-door case brought by a government's own ethics body, or a bid protest that opens the specification's drafting record.
items.would_refute: Emergency contracts, specification authorship and officials' next employers being published as they are awarded.

items.title: The crypto industry inside the legislatures and regulators writing its rules
items.claim: The exchanges and token issuers are probably inside legislatures and financial regulators well beyond the United States, because a licensing regime written to attract them is worth more than any amount spent getting it written.
items.rule: The map proves both halves separately: a regulator's chair arriving from the industry he then regulated, with that industry's lawsuits dropped afterwards, and a financier paying a small state's bank regulator to look away while his bank failed. Industry money is now among the largest single sources in several countries' election spending, which is the condition the map's proved vote-buying cases all share.
items.conditions: Jurisdictions compete openly to host these firms, so a regulator granting a licence is also an instrument of national policy. The licence is granted and withdrawn by the same small office, in places where that office and the industry share one professional world.
items.documented: The map holds a crypto adviser who became chair of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, after which crypto lawsuits were dropped; a United Arab Emirates spy chief's firm buying 49 percent of the Trump family crypto company; and Stanford paying Antigua's bank regulator to look away.
items.would_show: A licensing scandal with an official named, regulator staff prosecuted, or an audit of why one firm's licence survived a failure that closed others.
items.would_refute: Licence decisions, conditions, refusals and withdrawals being published with reasons.

items.title: The donor-funded policy shops that write a programme and then staff the government
items.claim: The pattern of a privately funded institute writing a government's programme and then supplying the people to run it is probably in use well beyond the two countries where it has been documented, because it is legal, repeatable and cheaper than a party.
items.rule: The map proves it four times over in detail, and the proof is unusually clean: the institutes published what they wanted, their people took the posts, and the measures were adopted. What makes it a possible pattern elsewhere is that the model is openly admired and openly funded, and that the countries where it has been documented are simply the ones with the most transparent appointment records.
items.conditions: A new government needs thousands of appointees and has no bench. An institute can offer vetted staff, a drafted programme and the donors behind both. Nothing requires an appointee's previous employer's funders to be disclosed.
items.documented: The map holds Heritage's 1981 Mandate for Leadership, with 60 percent of its 2,000 proposals acted on; Project 2025's authors staffing a second Trump term; PNAC's signatories taking ten posts in the government that fought the Iraq war; Nippon Kaigi members holding 15 of 19 seats in a Japanese cabinet and 10 of 19 in another; an agribusiness-funded institute drafting Brazil's farm caucus agenda; and a business chamber chief leading the consultation on Indonesia's omnibus jobs law.
items.would_show: An appointment record traced to an institute's roster, a drafting record showing an institute's text adopted, or a funding disclosure forced by a court or parliament.
items.would_refute: Appointment and drafting records being published, showing programmes written inside government by people it recruited itself.

items.title: The global consultancies inside the finance ministries of states they also sell to
items.claim: The large consultancies are probably inside the finance and privatisation ministries of more states than the prosecutions show, advising on sales, tax rules and restructurings while holding the bidders and the taxpayers affected as clients on the other side.
items.rule: The map proves the conflict being used, not merely existing: a partner leaking a government's own tax plans to colleagues who then marketed advice on them, and two of the firms paying officials at state companies they were advising. These came out through a parliamentary inquiry and a United States prosecution - neither of which is available in most of the countries where the same firms hold the same seats.
items.conditions: A ministry short of staff hires the firm that also serves the industry being regulated or sold. The engagement letter is not published, the firm's other clients are confidential, and the privatisation it advises on produces the bidders it already advises.
items.documented: The map holds McKinsey paying South African state-firm officials and settling for 122 million dollars; a PwC partner leaking Australian Treasury tax plans to colleagues; BCG's Lisbon office paying an agent 4.3 million dollars to win Angolan state contracts; gas firms paying a former Spanish minister's consultancy to get tax laws changed; and Rio Tinto's consultant offering a Guinean official 822,000 dollars over Simandou.
items.would_show: A parliamentary inquiry or audit office report on an engagement, a debarment, or a prosecution naming the ministry seat as well as the payment.
items.would_refute: Engagement letters, conflict waivers and the firms' other clients in the same sector being disclosed to the hiring ministry and published.

items.title: Conflict gold inside the central banks that buy it and the ministries that licence its export
items.claim: The networks moving artisanal and conflict gold are probably inside the central banks that buy it and the ministries that licence its export, because gold is the one commodity that needs a state signature to turn from loot into reserves.
items.rule: Unlike cocaine, gold has to be made legal somewhere: a refinery needs an export permit, and a central bank purchase programme turns informal metal into a national asset. That signature is the thing worth buying, and the map proves it being bought in two countries already. Gold has also become the preferred route for states and armed groups under sanctions, which raises what a permit is worth without changing who signs it.
items.conditions: Several producing states buy gold through the central bank or a state agent at a set price, and a small set of officials signs the export permits. The sums matter to a national balance sheet, which makes the arrangement politically protected rather than merely corrupt.
items.documented: The map holds the United States and United Kingdom sanctioning Kamlesh Pattni over bribes in Zimbabwe's gold trade, a United States Treasury finding that Zimbabwe's president shields gold and diamond smugglers and takes payments from them, and United States charges that the Mohamed gold family bribed Guyanese officials.
items.would_show: A sanctions designation naming a refinery together with a central bank officer, a parliamentary audit of a gold purchase programme, or a prosecution over export permits.
items.would_refute: Audits of the purchase programmes finding the metal and the permits accounted for.

items.title: The companies racing to plug in data centres, inside the bodies that decide grid connections
items.claim: The companies building data centres are probably reaching the small bodies that decide grid connections, tariffs and siting - in Ireland, the Gulf, Chile, Malaysia and the American states - because a single signature there is now worth billions.
items.rule: The mechanism is proved on this map in the same sector and the same country at a time when the prize was far smaller. What has changed is the size of the decision, not the size of the body taking it: a place in the interconnection queue, or a tariff written for one customer, is still settled by a handful of appointees on a commission or inside a grid operator.
items.conditions: A connection decision can move years of revenue and is often taken without a public hearing. The companies wanting the connection fund the politicians who appoint the commissioners, and the engineers who model the grid move between the operator and the firms queuing for it.
items.documented: The map holds FirstEnergy's 60 million dollar network for an Ohio bailout law, and the 4.3 million it paid to the man who then became Ohio's utility regulator. It also holds the revolving door at the top of the same sector: a fracking chief who became United States energy secretary, and an E.ON subsidiary chief who became Germany's energy minister.
items.would_show: An inspector-general or commission investigation into an interconnection or tariff decision, an ethics finding against a commissioner, or a leaked connection agreement with the terms in it.
items.would_refute: The large connection decisions turning out to be made on a published formula, with the queue and its exceptions open to inspection.
